questions.prompt: Order the layers from the base of the pyramid to the top (most tests to fewest).
questions.explanation: The base is many fast unit tests, then fewer integration tests, then the fewest, slowest end-to-end tests at the top.

questions.prompt: Why do we write fewer end-to-end tests than unit tests?

options.text: E2E tests can't find any real bugs
E2E tests are slower, costlier to maintain, and flakier, though more realistic
Unit tests give more confidence the whole system works

questions.explanation: Higher-layer tests are more realistic but slower, more brittle, and costlier, so you keep them few and focused on critical journeys.

options.text: Writing tests only for pure functions
An inverted pyramid: many slow E2E/manual tests and few unit tests

questions.explanation: The ice-cream cone is top-heavy — mostly slow, brittle end-to-end and manual tests with a thin base of unit tests.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the testing pyramid are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is a heuristic about proportions and cost, not an exact-ratio law
Ratios like 70/20/10 are illustrations, not rules
The testing trophy weights integration tests heavily for some contexts
Google's small/medium/large sizes contradict the pyramid's advice

questions.explanation: The pyramid is a heuristic; ratios are illustrative; the trophy re-weights toward integration; Google's sizes reinforce (not contradict) 'prefer smaller/faster tests'.

questions.prompt: A test that drives the whole system the way a real user would is called an ____ test (three letters / hyphenated).
questions.explanation: End-to-end (E2E) tests exercise the whole system like a user; they sit at the top of the pyramid.

questions.prompt: Match each test layer to a fitting example for a sign-up feature.

pairs.right: create_user() writes and reads a row in a test database
Fill the sign-up form in a browser and see 'Welcome'

questions.explanation: Pure logic is a unit test; code-plus-database is integration; a full browser journey is E2E; Google's sizes reframe the same gradient.
